RagShortTexts: Novgorod bark notes carry household, debt and delivery messages, sometimes through scribes.
Carriers add spoken news; deliveries still require the right recipient and actual fulfilment.

Variants.Content:
Novgorod bark notes carried household matters, debts, goods and commissions. A stylus could incise a short message on bark, while long books required more materials and writing labor. 

Sender, scribe, carrier and reader could be different people; literate relatives or trusted helpers enabled communication. Writing allowed instructions in someone’s absence, but recipients still needed to identify names, objects and the particular transaction meant.

A traveler could carry a bark note to a household, shop or acquaintance. An illiterate carrier relied on spoken instructions to identify the recipient; changed routes could delay or lose it. Private letter carriers arranged their own travel, lodging and mounts. With duplicate names or an unclear commission, finding a witness known to both parties was safer than handing over property immediately.

Merchants and notables could use bark notes for deliveries, debts or instructions to absent partners. Messages needed comparison with the actual handover: who sent the letter, who received goods and whether payment occurred affected claims and reputation. Trusted scribes and regular carriers maintained contact; recurring trade made handwriting and customary names familiar. Keeping a note helped, but goods, witnesses and performance remained central to disputes.

Relatives could send bark notes requesting clothes, money or assistance and ask literate friends to write or read them. This reached distant people but disclosed private matters to intermediaries. A few lines might omit background each side assumed the other knew. Recipients often asked carriers to distinguish written wording, spoken additions and news heard along the way.
